mcqs.question: An API gateway validates all incoming requests before forwarding them to internal services. Why should those internal services still validate their own inputs?
options: Because gateway validation always runs slower than service-level validation
Because internal services are legally required to duplicate all validation logic
Because gateways cannot technically perform validation on JSON payloads

Because internal services can be reached by other callers besides the gateway, and gateway logic could itself have a gap — treating one validation point as sufficient turns any bypass into a system-wide exposure
mcqs.explanation: A trust boundary exists wherever data crosses into a new component's control, and relying on a single upstream check means any bypass or gap there removes protection for every downstream service at once. This isn't about performance or a legal requirement, and gateways validate JSON payloads without issue — the reasoning is architectural, not technical limitation.

mcqs.question: A search field blocks the literal string `<script>` to prevent XSS, but allows everything else through. What kind of gap does this leave?
options: A blocklist gap — variants like different capitalization, a different tag, or an encoded form can bypass a check for one exact string, since the list only covers what someone thought to add
None — blocking that specific string fully prevents any script injection
This is an allowlist approach and is therefore already maximally safe
The gap only exists in server-rendered pages, never in single-page applications
mcqs.explanation: Blocklists only cover known-bad patterns explicitly listed, so any variation not on that list — capitalization, a different tag, encoding — passes through untouched, which is exactly why allowlisting is preferred. This is a blocklist, not an allowlist, one exact-string block doesn't prevent all script injection, and the gap isn't limited to any particular rendering approach.

mcqs.question: A team sanitizes user comments by stripping HTML tags when the comment is saved to the database. They later render that same comment inside a JavaScript string in a different part of the app and get an XSS vulnerability. What went wrong?
options: HTML sanitization is never effective under any circumstances
The database itself failed to store the sanitized value correctly

Sanitizing at input time doesn't protect every future output context; encoding needs to happen at output time, matched to the specific context (HTML vs. JavaScript string) the data is being placed into
Validation and sanitization are the same operation, so this indicates a validation library bug
mcqs.explanation: Sanitizing for one context (removing HTML tags) doesn't make a value safe in a different context (a JavaScript string), because each output context has different characters that matter — that's why contextual output encoding, not one-time input sanitization, is the actual defense against XSS. HTML sanitization does work for its intended context, this isn't a database storage issue, and validation and sanitization are explicitly different operations.

mcqs.question: A developer says a form field is safe because the browser's JavaScript rejects invalid input before submission. Why is this not a security control?
options: Browsers execute JavaScript in a random order, so validation might not run every time
JavaScript validation is always removed automatically after page load
An attacker can send a request directly to the server, bypassing the browser and its JavaScript entirely, so that validation never runs for that request at all
JavaScript cannot check string length or format under any circumstances
mcqs.explanation: An attacker isn't limited to using the form — a direct request via curl, a script, or a modified request bypasses client-side JavaScript entirely, which is why the server must enforce every security-relevant check independently. Browsers don't run JS in random order, JS isn't auto-removed after load, and JavaScript is fully capable of checking length and format — the issue is that it's optional from the attacker's side, not a technical limitation.

mcqs.question: Why should an internal service validate input from another internal service it trusts, rather than skipping validation for "trusted" internal calls?
options: Internal services are contractually required to validate all traffic under most compliance frameworks
Internal network traffic is always slower than external traffic, so validation adds negligible overhead
Kubernetes automatically disables validation for services in the same namespace
If the calling service is ever compromised, skipping validation means every service that blindly trusts it inherits that compromise immediately, with nothing standing in the way
mcqs.explanation: Trusting an internal caller by network position or team ownership, rather than by actually checking what it sends, means a single compromised service can propagate its compromise unchecked — the same reasoning that motivates zero trust at the network layer. This isn't primarily a compliance mandate, has nothing to do with relative traffic speed, and Kubernetes has no such automatic behavior.

mcqs.question: A system validates all input at its API gateway and every downstream service assumes that validation already happened. A new internal caller is later added that bypasses the gateway entirely. What's the consequence?
options: None, because the gateway's validation rules are automatically copied to every internal service
Every downstream service that skipped its own validation, relying solely on the gateway, is now exposed to that new caller with no validation defense at all
The new caller will automatically be rejected by the network layer
Only the gateway itself becomes vulnerable; downstream services remain protected
mcqs.explanation: Once a caller bypasses the single validation point a system relied on exclusively, every service that skipped its own checks has no remaining defense — this is exactly the risk of treating one upstream check as sufficient instead of validating at every trust boundary. Validation rules aren't automatically propagated, the network layer doesn't reject callers based on missing validation, and it's the downstream services (not just the gateway) that end up exposed.
